prompt: What question is a scatterplot built to answer?

choices.text: How a total splits into parts
choices.why: That is a part-to-whole question, for a stacked bar or a pie.
Right. One quantity per axis, one point per item.
That is a bar chart's question.

choices.text: How one quantity is spread out
choices.why: That is a histogram's question, lesson 5.

prompt: Which variable goes on the horizontal axis, by convention?

choices.text: The one that might explain the other
choices.why: Right. Distance across, time up.

choices.text: The one with the larger numbers
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it.
That one goes up, where readers expect the outcome.
The order of measurement does not decide the axes.

prompt: A scatterplot shows that stores with more parking spaces sell more. A director wants to build parking everywhere. What is the first thing to say?

choices.text: The trend line should be removed
choices.why: The line is not the problem; the reading of it is.
Right. Bigger stores in bigger places would have both.

choices.text: The axes are the wrong way round
choices.why: Swapping them would not change what the chart can show.
They are the best chart for showing one. They cannot show why.

prompt: Why can 46 deliveries with 8 items look like one point?

choices.why: Every point was drawn; they just landed in the same column.

choices.text: They are drawn over each other
choices.why: Right. That is overplotting.
It draws every point it is given.
Eight is the most common basket size here.

prompt: Which of these reduce overplotting? Choose every one that applies.

choices.why: Right. Piles become darker spots.

choices.text: Count the points in a grid and colour the cells
choices.why: Right, for very large data.

choices.text: Draw the points larger so they are easier to see
choices.why: Larger points overlap more.
Right, by less than the gap between real values.

prompt: When is jitter honest?

choices.text: Whenever it makes the chart look less crowded
choices.why: Looking less crowded is not the test; moved too far, a point seems to have another value.
It moves the drawing, not the data, and within a gap nobody misreads it.

choices.text: When the shift stays within the gap
choices.why: Right. Then no point lands in a neighbour's column.
It belongs on whichever axis has the repeated values.

prompt: A state with four times another's orders gets a bubble with what radius?

choices.why: That gives sixteen times the area.
That would be 256 times the area.

choices.text: The same radius, in a darker colour
choices.why: Then the size would carry nothing.
Right. Four times the area is twice the radius.

prompt: In a bubble chart, which variable should go into the bubble's area?

choices.text: The most important one, so it stands out
choices.why: The most important deserves the best channel, which is position.

choices.text: The one with the largest numbers
choices.why: The size of the numbers does not decide the channel.

choices.text: The one where a rough sense is enough
choices.why: Right. Area is read poorly; the precise comparisons go on the axes.
Area carries amounts; categories want hue or shape.

prompt: Why draw the largest bubbles first?

choices.text: So they do not cover the small ones
choices.why: Right. Drawn last, a big bubble hides what is behind it.

choices.text: So the reader sees them first
choices.why: The reader sees them first anyway; they are the biggest.
Software draws in whatever order it is given.

choices.text: To make the chart load faster
choices.why: The order does not change the speed.

prompt: The fitted line was minutes = 22.8 + 2.17 × km. What does it predict for a 10 km delivery, in minutes, to one decimal place?
The correlation was 0.88 and its square 0.78. What does 0.78 mean?

choices.text: 78% of the deliveries lie on the line
choices.why: Almost no point lies exactly on the line.
It measures association, not cause.
Right. The other 22% is rain, basket size and chance.
The slope is 2.17 minutes per km, a different number.

prompt: The line predicts 153 minutes for a 60 km delivery. Why should nobody quote that number?

choices.why: Right. That is extrapolation, beyond anything measured.
It is a good summary inside the data.

choices.text: 153 minutes is too long for a delivery
choices.why: Long or short, the issue is that nothing was measured there.

choices.text: The correlation is too low to predict anything
choices.why: 0.88 is high; the problem is the distance, not the fit.

prompt: City deliveries and countryside deliveries each show time rising with distance, but one line through both falls. What should you do?

choices.text: Colour the two groups and fit each one
choices.why: Right. Mixing groups can reverse the trend each shows.

choices.text: Trust the single line, since it uses all the data
choices.why: Using all the data is exactly what produced the misleading line.
Removing a group hides it rather than explaining the pattern.
A log axis does not separate groups.

prompt: On a logarithmic axis, what do equal distances mean?

choices.why: That is an ordinary axis.
The axis spacing has nothing to do with how many points there are.
Right. 100 to 1,000 is as far as 10,000 to 100,000.
A share of the total is not what the spacing encodes.

prompt: Why can a bar chart not use a logarithmic value axis?

choices.text: Its bars would have no base to stand on
choices.why: Right. The bar's length would mean nothing.
Columns are vertical bars; orientation is not the issue.
They apply to any positive quantity.
Many tools will draw it; it is still meaningless.

prompt: São Paulo had 61,040 orders and Roraima 140. How many times Roraima's orders did São Paulo have, to the nearest whole number?
Find each of these in the scatterplot.

labels.text: the densest part of the cloud

prompt: Match each problem to its fix.

pairs.left: points pile up on repeated values

pairs.right: a dashed line and a warning

prompt: Put the four things to read in a scatterplot in the order the lesson reads them.
Drawing a trend line beyond the range of the data is called ___.
A chart plots sales against advertising for 27 states on log axes, without saying so. A reader says the gap between two states looks small. What is the risk?

choices.text: Log axes hide states with zero sales
choices.why: True, but it is not what this reader is getting wrong.
The issue is how gaps are read, not the shape of the trend.

choices.text: A small gap there means a tenfold difference
choices.why: Right. Readers read distances as differences unless told otherwise.

choices.text: None; the tick labels make it clear
choices.why: Many readers never look at tick labels closely, which is why the lesson asks for words.
